hlni.insight: A short illustrative activity can reveal where you need help or what you want to investigate next; it cannot determine which degree suits you.
hlni.audienceGap: The student believes they must 'know' which degree is right before starting.
hlni.viewerChange: Shifts from guessing based on labels to investigating based on personal learning hurdles.
hlni.support: The observation belongs to the specific task performance, helping the student identify what they actually want to learn.
hlni.payoff: The student produces a specific, actionable question that helps them evaluate any programme objectively.

candidate.reelTitle: B.Com vs BBA: Finding Your Focus
candidate.objective: Help students move from degree-label anxiety to identifying specific academic research questions.
candidate.targetAudience: +2 students seeking accessible, supportive guidance, including students worried about marks, confidence, or belonging

shots.name: The Dilemma
shots.visual: A student sits at a desk, looking frustrated at two open books labeled B.Com and BBA. They push the books away.
shots.dialogue: Choosing between B.Com and BBA feels like a massive gamble, doesn't it?
shots.cameraPerformance: Close-up on the student's face, showing genuine uncertainty.

shots.name: The Method
shots.visual: The student tries a short resource allocation case study on their laptop and writes in a journal. We see the text clearly.
shots.dialogue: Try a brief case study. I got stuck here: 'How to justify resource limits.' Now I have a real question.
shots.cameraPerformance: Over-the-shoulder shot focusing on the journal entry.

shots.name: The Payoff
shots.visual: Student looks at the camera, then down at their specific research question written on a sticky note.
shots.dialogue: Instead of guessing, ask: How does the programme teach the process of defining constraints for resource models?

productionNotes.editing: Steady, focused on the transition from frustration to clarity.

creativeSummary.keyCreativeIdea: Transforming the abstract anxiety of choosing a degree into a concrete research activity using a task journal.
shootingPriority: The student's direct address to camera

selected.title: The Sticking Point Journal
selected.audienceGap: Feeling overwhelmed by the pressure to choose the 'correct' degree path.
selected.hlni: A short illustrative activity can reveal where you need help or what you want to investigate next; it cannot determine which degree suits you.
selected.viewerChange: Moves from feeling pressured to choosing to feeling empowered to investigate specific task challenges.
selected.concept: Two students discussing a task; one records a moment where they felt stuck, turning a moment of frustration into a productive research question.
selected.device: A physical journal entry shown on camera capturing a specific hurdle during a sample exercise.
selected.support: The observation belongs to this activity and participant; it supports a next question rather than a general prediction.
methodSteps: Try or inspect a clearly illustrative task.
Record one point where you needed help and one question you want to investigate.
Turn the observation into a question for a real course brief or course team.
selected.interpretationRule: Use the recorded observation to choose the next question, not to select a degree from one activity.
selected.visibleProof: A person records a specific sticking point and asks a different, more useful question afterward.
selected.payoff: Use the recorded observation to choose the next question, not to select a degree from one activity.
selected.limitations: A brief exercise does not measure aptitude, learning style, long-term interest or academic performance.

demonstration.input: A brief, clearly illustrative case study task involving resource allocation.
demonstration.observation: Student writes down: 'I struggled to justify the allocation of resources without a clear limit'.
demonstration.nextQuestion: How does the programme teach the process of defining constraints for resource models?

comparedWith.hlni: A task label alone does not tell you what you must produce, what will be assessed, or what feedback you receive. Ask these as separate questions.
comparedWith.device: Split-screen view of two worksheets where the student fills in columns for 'Work Product,' 'Criterion,' and 'Available Feedback.'

comparedWith.hlni: The same total can result from different component values; an aggregate alone cannot tell you the underlying mix.

conceptSelection.contrast: The selected mechanisms provide distinct ways to handle uncertainty: 'Trust' focuses on auditing workload (Assessment Audit), 'Connection' focuses on identifying personal research gaps (Task Journaling), and 'Discovery' focuses on mathematically demonstrating why labels are often misleading (Aggregate Counterexample).
